vignette:
Thomas traces the beginning of the end to a Tuesday night fourteen months ago. He, his wife, and their four-year-old daughter had just finished dinner when the back door splintered open. The two men who entered were not just intruders; for the next seven hours, they were gods, and his home was their universe. The event itself is a collection of searingly vivid fragments that ambush him without warning. He remembers the specific, acrid smell of burning plastic as one of them held a lighter to his daughter's doll, the demand for his investment bank's security codes, and the chilling, unnatural silence that fell between their threats. But the memory that feels more real than his own reflection is the sound of his daughter's weeping from the closet they'd locked her in-a thin, terrified sound he was powerless to stop. He complied with every demand, emptied his accounts, and begged for his family's lives, feeling a part of himself curdle into shame. He had come to believe that in those hours, he failed a fundamental test of manhood, acting not as a protector but as a pliant object, a tool for their enrichment.

In the aftermath, the world rearranged itself around the axis of that night. The police investigation yielded nothing; the men were never found, a fact that lodges in Thomas's mind as a profound injustice, proof that the world is lawless and he is alone in his watchfulness. His own home, the site of the violation, became an outpost he had to guard relentlessly. Sleep became a dereliction of duty. He lies awake for hours each night, cataloging the building's groans and the city's distant hum, certain that relaxing his guard is an invitation for disaster to strike again. He feels not tired, but brittle, a wire pulled too taut. His work as a financial analyst, once a source of pride, now offers new terrain for terror. The intense quiet of the trading floor during moments of high concentration feels identical to the dreadful silence the intruders used to exert control. He often has to flee his desk for the noise of the coffee machine, his heart hammering against his ribs, just to escape the feeling of suffocating anticipation.

The deepest fractures appeared in his marriage. His wife, trying to offer comfort, would reach for him, but her touch felt like a prelude to violence. A simple hug would send a jolt of panic through him, and he would recoil as if from a hot flame. He saw the hurt in her eyes morph into confusion, and then into a weary distance he could no longer cross. He felt like a ghost in his own life, a shell of a person going through the motions, and he couldn't explain why the very affection he craved felt like a threat. The divorce was finalized six months ago. Now, he lives in a new apartment, but the feeling of being unsafe followed him, a permanent tenant in his mind. He avoids parks and family restaurants, anywhere he might hear a child crying, a sound that instantly transports him back to the closet door, to the feeling of absolute helplessness. He has come to see himself as fundamentally changed, no longer a person but a collection of damaged responses.

It was a visit with his daughter last week that finally propelled him to seek help. She had scraped her knee and was crying, and when he bent to comfort her, she reached up to hug him. For a split second, he flinched away before he could stop himself. The look on her face-not of fear, but of simple, heartbreaking confusion-was more than he could bear. He realized that the perimeter he was guarding was no longer just his apartment; it was his own heart, and he was keeping the one person he loved most on the outside. He is here not with any grand hope of reclaiming his old self, who he now sees as a naive stranger, but with the desperate, flickering wish to one day hold his daughter without the fear that he will break.
